newsitem.title: UK: Dollar steady in Europe, stg rallies on UK reforms.
newsitem.headline: Dollar steady in Europe, stg rallies on UK reforms.

text.p: The dollar steadied in Europe after an overnight roller-coaster ride, while sterling stole the limelight and rallied sharply on a quarter-point rise in UK interest rates and news of policy independence for the Bank of England.

Sterling rose almost two pfennigs and more than one cent after new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown announced the expected rate rise in tandem with a new freedoms for the central bank to decide future interest rate moves.
Brown made the announcement after his first meeting with Bank of England governor Eddie George since the Labour Party victory in last week's UK election.

"The market is looking more at the BOE independence measures than the rate rise and the forex market at least is taking the view that this will mean a tighter overall monetary policy than previously seen," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston.

Brown said the UK Treasury would set the inflation target and reaffirmed the existing 2.5 percent goal. He said a nine-man central bank council, partly appointed by the Chancellor, will then have freedom to vote on the appropriate interest rates needed to meet that inflation target.
At 1112 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.7286/91 marks compared with 1.7283/88 late Monday.
Sterling/mark rose to 2.8245/55 marks compared with 2.7935/45 late Monday.

UK government bonds and stocks rallied sharply on the view that greater independence for the central bank will be lower UK inflation over the long-term, analysts said. However, they said the measures were still short of the central bank reforms needed to take part in European monetary union.

The UK move overshadowed a slew of German economic data, meantime. Although the economic reports released today showed a pick-up in activity, the dollar/mark rate was little moved and was even helped higher later by sterling/mark, traders said.

German industrial orders rose 1.1 percent in March while the German Purchasing Managers sentiment index rose two points to 56.58 in April. A seasonally-adjusted 8,000 rise in German unemployment was slightly less than the 15,000 rise expected but in line with unadjusted figures leaked on Monday.

"Any strength in the German data, particularly the export side of the industrial numbers, has been due largely to the rising dollar/mark," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch. "Neither the German government nor the Bundesbank will want to bite the hand that feeds."
The latest Bundesbank comments signalled no rate changes.
Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said he saw no need for interest rate rises at present.

Despite the rise in German economic activity, jitters about an interest rate rise in Japan are more pronounced and the yen gained against both the dollar and mark overnight while Japanese government bond yields pushed higher.

The higher sensitivity of the yen to rate rise talk is partly because cheap yen borrowings have been used by investors around the world over the past year to fund high-yield holdings. Any prospect of a change in the cost of yen borrowing prompts profit taking on these positions, analysts said.

"There seems to be a consensus building that G3 rate rises will be staggered and quite far apart - the U.S. has already moved, the pressure in Japan is building and continental Europe will lag for some time," said a senior trader at a U.S. bank here. "Mark/yen is very vulnerable in that set up and sterling looks as good as ever."
At 1140 GMT, the mark/yen cross was at 72.73/75 compared with 73.17/20 late Monday.
